Paśupati
------------------------------------------
Paśupati is one of the names of Lord शिव. A जीव who is bound by the पाश or bondage of इग्नोरन्चे and sees himself as the body-मिन्द् complex is called ‘paśu’. शिव being the lord of all such paśus (or jīvas), can rightly be called ‘Paśupati’.
Paśupati is one of the eight aspects or forms of रुद्र-शिव. In this aspect, he is a deity of the plants and has स्वाहा as his divine consort. He is also the lord of quadrupeds and bipeds (vide Taittirīya Saṁhitā

.11 and 12). Iconographically, he is shown like शिव with four hands, carrying a sword and a shield in the two upper hands, the lower two hands showing the mudras (or poses) of abhaya (protection) and varada (giving boons).
Paśupatinātha is the presiding deity of Nepal.

pāṣaṇḍin
(‘heretic’)
------------------------------------------
‘Pā’ means ‘to protect’. ‘Ṣaṇḍ’ means ‘to revile’. Hence the word literally means ‘one who reviles’. In practice, it was used to indicate all persons who reviled the वेदस् (or did not believe in them) which alone can protect the human beings (according to the believers) by spiritually elevating them.
Several sects such as Kāpāla, Nākula (Pāśupata), Vāma, भैरव, कालामुख (and even the Pāñcarātra!) were branded as avaidika (not sanctioned by the वेदस् or against the Vedic tradition) and pāṣaṇḍa. The followers of these sects were called pāṣaṇḍins or pākhaṇḍins which word also means the same thing.
The lists often included the Jains and the Buddhists also.
The पुराणस् like the Kūrma contain highly derogatory statements against the pāṣaṇḍins and forbid any association with them.

Paśupatinātha Temple
------------------------------------------
One of the most important places of पिल्ग्रिमगे associated with Lord शिव is the पशुपतिनाथ तेम्प्ले in Nepal.
Paśupatinātha Temple at NepalNepal, got its name by its association with a great sage called ‘Nemi मुनि’ (Skāndapurāṇa, Himavatkhaṇḍa, 11.60). He is said to have lived near this temple and taken care of it.
Nepal is full of हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्, of which the temple of Paśupatinātha is the most important and the holiest. According to the local traditions it is at least 1500 years old.
The legend goes that Lord शिव and his divine spouse पार्वती, while wandering in the हिमालयस् came here, liked the place very much and settled down as a ‘mṛga and mṛgī’ (deer-couple). When the gods of हेअवेन् started searching for the ‘missing’ couple, they found a strange deer with one horn and three eyes, moving about, along with a female deer. Recognising them as शिव and पार्वती, the gods tried to take them back to कैलास (the abode of शिव) but failed. शिव gave up the deer form, assumed the jyotirliṅga shape (liṅga of light) and settled down on the bank of river Bāgmatī (now in Kāṭhmaṇḍu, the capital of Nepal).
Since he had assumed the shape of a पशु or animal, but is really the pati or Lord of all livings beings, he is known as ‘Paśupati’ or ‘Paśupatinātha’.
The Nepālamāhātmya (1

) of the work mentioned earlier, declares that this temple of Paśupatinātha is surrounded by the rivers Kauśikī, Triśūlagaṅgā and another ‘holy river with cold waters’. ‘Śivapurī’ (Kailāsa mountain?) is towards the north.
The temple was destroyed by the Muslim invaders in A.
but was rebuilt by the king Jayasiṁharāma. The present structure was built in A.

in two stories since the old one was destroyed by white ants!
The लिङ्ग in the main shrine is made of black stone and has four faces. Each has a pair of hands in different mudras (poses). The scalps have matted hair on the three faces and the fourth face—half man and half woman—is that of अर्ध-नारीश्वर.

Pāśupatasūtras
------------------------------------------
One of the—or, perhaps, the chief-basic texts of the—Pāśupata शैविस्म् is the Pāśupatasūtras (2nd cent. A. D.) with the bhāṣya (commentary) of Kauṇḍinya (4th to 6th cent. A. D.). Since five subjects viz., कार्य (effect), कारण (cause), योग (meditation and union), विधि (behaviour) and duḥkhānta (dissolution of sorrow) have been discussed, this work is also known as the Pañcārthasūtras.
Only a ब्राह्मण with keen senses was considered as fit for the path of spiritual discipline described here.
The work lays great emphasis on ascetic forms of discipline. पशुपति’s or ईश्वर’s grace is absolutely necessary to attain duḥkhānta (same as मोक्ष).
See also ŚAIVISM.

paśyantī
------------------------------------------
It is the second stage of manifestation of sound or speech from the first unmanifest state (called ‘parā’).
See under TANTRAS.

paścāt-tāpa
(‘feeling remorse afterwards’)
------------------------------------------
The topic of sins and their expiations is often discussed in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. They recognise that human beings are prone, due to the evil सṁस्कारस् or past impressions and habits, to commit sins.
The first and foremost step in the expiation of sins is to realise one’s mistake and repent for the same. This repentance, since it comes after (= paścāt) the deed is committed, is called ‘paścāt-tāpa’.
If this paścāttāpa is intense, that itself may be considered—at least in some cases—as sufficient प्रायश्चित्त or expiation.

paśu
(‘animal’)
------------------------------------------
The ignorant जीव or सोउल् who is bound to the cycle of transmigration is called ‘paśu’.
See ŚAIVISM.

pāśa
(‘that which binds’, ‘noose’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word ‘pāśa’ stands for anything that binds (including emotional attachments) it is used more in a technical sense to indicate the lasso or a long rope with a noose, shown in the hands of certain deities like यम (the god of death) and वरुण (the god of fate and punishment). Many other deities like गणपति and some aspects of the देवी are also shown with it.
Pāśa invariably goes with aṅkuśa (goad), the deities holding them both. Generally the aṅkuśa is held in the right hand and the पाश in the left.
These two signify the controlling and the binding power of the deity.
Iconographical works show them in a variety of ways.
Symbolically, पाश stands for attachment or desire and aṅkuśa for anger.
